https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/.text: Salford Quays has to be one of Greater Manchester’s most unique places to visit. Where else can you find watersports, striking modern architecture, TV studios and an island full of gnomes? Oh, and it also happens to be home to the beach - well, of sorts. More on that later. My visit to Salford Quays did get off to an interesting start thanks to a visit to the Quayside Shopping Mall. Nipping inside to use the facilities, I can see why this place is often called a ‘ghost’ shopping centre. Click here for the latest on Manchester's food & drink scene, gigs and more in our CityLife newsletter I walked past vacant shop after vacant shop, marvelling at how barren the place felt and if I’m being honest, slightly creepy too. Previously called The Lowry Outlet Mall, it was rebanded as Quayside in 2020. Some big brands still remain like the M&S Outlet and the food area is going strong. In recent years the mall has welcomed new additions like the Oxygen play centre and Kargo MKT, a popular spot for those heading to a gig at Victoria Warehouse. But the future is looking rather different for Quayside with a £16million overhaul planned. This includes the addition of a Hollywood Bowl bowling alley which has recently been given the green light, and is estimated to open in 2028. It’s set to be joined by a ‘cutting edge’ electric GoKarting track by international firm Hyperdrive Karting. But for now it still feels rather empty, so departing Quayside shopping mall with a feeling of relief, I set out to explore Salford Quays, heading in the direction of the aforementioned ‘beach’. Crossing the Plaza, I strolled past the Lowry, a striking building constructed from steel designed to look like a ship in the docks, a reminder of the area’s history and how this area has undergone a rebirth. Walking around Salford Quays today with its fancy flats and tree-lined promenades, it’s hard to imagine what this area was once like. In fact it was once the third busiest port in Britain; the Manchester Ship Canal connected the city with Liverpool, allowing ocean-bound cargo vessels to travel to and from the city, often heading to Canada. Made up of nine docks in Salford, Stretford and Manchester, the Port of Manchester operated from 1894 until their closure in 1982, after the docks rapidly declined in the 1970s, largely due to containerisation. Regeneration began when Salford City Council acquired parts of the docks in 1983, launching the Salford Quays Development Plan in 1985. Under the scheme the docks were modified to create roads, bridges and landscaped waterfronts, and watersports facilities, moorings, houses and offices soon followed. Walking beside the water today, Salford Quays couldn’t be further away from its industrial past. But its rapid regeneration does reflect the rather surreal feeling this place gives you. It’s a place that has a sort of ‘Disneyland’ feeling to it, somewhere feels manufactured rather than a place that’s slowly evolved with time. Even the names of the areas have a whiff of North America about them: Harbour City, Ontario Basin, Clippers Quay. Although this is entirely by design - many of the basins are named after places in Canada to reflect the ship routes. Yet it’s this purposeful design which also gives Salford Quays a sense of fun. Take its various footbridges; where else would you find so many colourful and quirky water crossings in Greater Manchester? A personal favourite is the Detroit Bridge, instantly recognisable thanks to its red, white and blue steel framing. On my walk to my first stop of the day, I crossed a small yet playful pale blue bridge which really wouldn’t look out of place in Disneyland. It’s here that I passed Salford Watersports Centre and Agecroft Rowing Club. It was a bit too early in the day for them to be in full swing, but the watersports centre does offer a range of activities including kayaking, open water swimming and paddle boarding - which I’ve previously tried before at this very location and can safely say is brilliant. Eventually, after passing a rather unsettling number of geese, I arrived at the ‘beach’. Well I’m using the term beach in the loosest sense of the word. It’s a sandy embankment nestled beside Clippers Quay that’s completely inaccessible to the public, although it’s very popular with water fowl. Still, it’s sparked attention on TikTok so and I suppose at the right angle - if you avoid looking at all the washed-up detritus in the sand - it’s reminiscent of a small beach and great for bird spotters. Walk a little further up and you’ll come across trendy bar Bee Orchid and the Cult & Coffee Listening Cafe coffee shop, as well as a smattering of picnic benches popular with office workers at lunch times. From here I actually crossed into another borough completely, walking over the Trafford Road Swing Bridge. Heading over towards the Wharfside Metrolink stop, it meant I had the perfect vantage point to admire the fascinating place that is Gnome Island. It’s been a feature since 2017 when the first Gnome appeared on one of the derelict concrete islands in the docks. No one knows who’s behind it but it certainly puts a smile on the face of passers-by - and passengers on board the Salford Quays River Cruise. My next stop was the Imperial War Museum North, housed in a magnificent yet unsettling building constructed of three ‘shards’. It was designed by Berlin-based architect Daniel Libeskind. Born in Poland in 1946, dozens of his relatives had been murdered in The Holocaust. Standing beside the building it does feel imposing and its presence weighs upon you. Given its huge size, I was surprised that the entrance was a small door hidden on the other side away from the water, giving you the feeling that you’re entering a much darker world. The museum is completely free to visit and is open every day from 10am to 5pm, except from December 24 to 26. It takes you through the history of warfare in the 20th and 21st centuries, spanning the First World War to 9/11, via permanent displays and changing exhibitions. The current exhibition is Spies, Lies and Deception which, as you might have guessed, looks at the world of espionage. It’s a fascinating collection of real life stories and artefacts, including match boxes used to communicate secret messages and moulds designed to disguise footprints. Entering the main exhibition space, I was startled by a huge Harrier aircraft suspended from the ceiling which takes your breath away, depending on whether you’re into aviation or concerned about how structurally sound the support is. The space is then split up into different ‘silos’ which each focus on an aspect, including technology, communication and women at war. You can explore the museum at your own pace and the displays allow you to get up close to a vast selection of artefacts. As well as the Harrier aircraft, other large items on display include a British nuclear bomb, a piece of wreckage from the September 11 attacks on New York’s World Trade Centre, and an East German Trabant. One display which particularly caught my eye was on nuclear war, it includes a rather depressing map showing the nuclear fallout range of a bomb dropped in Manchester (spoiler alert: it’s not good). Heading back out into the sunshine, it was time for a bite to eat. I crossed the bridge over to Media City, casting a fleeting glance over to the ITV Studios and the hidden set of Coronation Street, and headed to Mattina Coffee located on Blue Road. An Italian deli-turned-coffee shop, it specialises in focaccia sandwiches, lasagne, fresh coffee pastries, including generously-filled cannoli. Given that I arrived at lunchtime, the place was full of Media City employees sporting lanyards of various colours, but I still managed to grab a table. Feeling hungry, I chose a mozzarella, mortadella and pesto focaccia sandwich (£7.50), a slice of lemon and olive oil cake (£4), a pistachio amaretti biscuit (£3) and an Americano £3. They also do a £9 lunch deal where you can get a sandwich, crisps or a mini cannolo and a soft drink, an option that was popular among the Media City workers. Sitting down with my lunch, I realised that my eyes were certainly greedier than my stomach. The sandwich was massive and could easily feed two, although I imagine it would be challenging to share given how delicious it was. The focaccia was crisp on the outside with a sprinkling of salt, while the inside was soft and springy. The fillings were generous, although slightly messy and the ham did slide around a little. But the flavours were fresh and worked well together - I was just sad I couldn’t have finished it all. Moving on to the cake, it was moist and citrusy with an excellent ratio of frosting contrasting with the tangy lemon flavours. The only criticism is that the edges were a bit over-done and a tad dry. The coffee was beautiful, full-bodied and complemented the sweet cake perfectly. I saved the amaretti for later and it was the perfect small sweet treat - I can imagine it being popular with those purchasing a morning coffee or an afternoon pick-me-up. The almond biscuit came topped with a dollop of pistachio cream. Not too sweet, it had a delicate nutty flavour and slightly crumbly texture which melted in the mouth. Mattina Coffee was the ideal way to round off my visit to Salford Quays. Although as I left I did catch sight of a few diners demolishing portions of lasagna, and despite feeling stuff I couldn’t help but look longlying at them. Looks like I’ll be coming back. Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/Reuters Gaza ‘Shameful’: UK, Australia and Canada criticise Israel over Gaza aid convoy killings decision Joint statement issued after IDF said it will not pursue criminal investigations into April 2024 strike that killed seven humanitarian workers Jason Burke Fri 21 Aug 2026 11.03 EDT First published on Fri 21 Aug 2026 10.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Britain, Australia and Canada have called the decision of the Israeli military authorities not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of aid vehicles in Gaza “shameful”. The strikes killed seven humanitarian workers from the US-based World Central Kitchen (WCK) organisation. WCK staff from the three countries were among the casualties of the attack, which prompted global outrage. “This decision is both too little, and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf. The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability,” the countries’ joint statement said . It continued: “In Gaza , humanitarian workers continue to work tirelessly to support civilians in desperate need, risking their lives whilst working in the most perilous conditions. Yet despite the fragile ceasefire, Gaza remains the deadliest place to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.” On Thursday, Australia’s government expressed “outrage” over the decision, while relatives said that Zomi Frankcom, the Australian among those killed, deserved more than an “internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.” Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision. The Polish government said on Thursday it was “very disappointed” and called for Israeli authorities to cooperate with Polish investigations into the incident. Damian Soból, a volunteer from Przemyśl, was also among the casualties. In London, the Foreign Office said the UK was “appalled and angry” for the families of John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby, three British citizens who were killed in the attack. WCK, which distributed food in Gaza throughout the war, said immediately after the lethal attack that it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement. The IDF said on Wednesday that it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the WCK convoy had deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded. One of the officers who was dismissed had reportedly signed an open letter earlier that year calling for Gaza to be deprived of aid. Israel imposed strict restrictions on the entry of humanitarian assistance during the conflict in Gaza, where experts declared a famine in August 2025. The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday that its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing, as well as into the fatal shooting of 15 paramedics in 2025. Hind Rajab died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as they sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed. The IDF repeatedly denied its troops had been in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible. The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”, but experts said criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians very rarely lead to convictions. Home Paid news feed Foto Agerpres Press Monitoring Bucharest Phone: +4 021.2076.110 Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve Day, celebrated by authorities, researchers, civil society Category: English Date: 2026-09-01 18:41:36 Foto: Luisiana BIGEA / AGERPRES Authorities, researchers and representatives of the business community and civil society participated on Tuesday in a meeting organised under the Danubius-RI project, a pan-European research project, with the declared purpose of involving the local communities of the Delta in the protection of the environment for the creation of a tool for sustainable management of the area. The event was organised by the Danube Delta National Institute for Research and Development (INCDDD) and the Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve Administration (DAHRA) as 36 years ago the Danube Delta and the other adjacent units were included in the international network of biosphere reserves, within the UNESCO program 'Man and the Biosphere', and September 1 was declared the day of the reserve, given that in 2008, on this day, a government decision by which the area is recognised as such came into force. During the meeting dubbed 'Delta in data and community - Citizen Observatory', the researchers presented the status of the Danubius-RI project, as well as that of the fulfilment of the Romanian components under the initiative Danubius-RO, with the authorities underlying the importance of September 1 and the need to get local communities and business operators involved as information about the ecosystems of the reserve is fragmented, and the area is complex. 'Without communities we cannot achieve this approach. We believe that the transformation of field observations into scientific information is the central pillar under the Danubius Ro-2 project and a process is needed that the entire community must understand in order to integrate the environmental monitoring components and this is the approach we are doing today, to create a Danubius citizen observatory,' said the scientific director of INCDDD, Iulian Nichersu, during the meeting. Danubius Citizen Observatory thus aims to be an instrument for the sustainable management of the Delta, by developing a participatory monitoring model, useful for both science and management and public policies. Also, representatives of civil society expressed their openness to participate in the initiative. 'Everything that means the involvement of stakeholders from rural communities can also be a contribution in the projects we are talking about and that is why we are interested,' said the representative of the Danube Delta Local Action Group, Roxana Iacob. In fact, some local action groups in Tulcea County have carried out projects on European funds dedicated to the study of climate change, implicitly to the protection of the environment and the communities in the reserve. The events dedicated to the reserve will continue on Tuesday, at the Jean Bart Theatre House with the free screening of the film 'Wild Delta', directed by Dan Dinu, which will be preceded by the opening of a photography exhibition dedicated to the area. 'We have been working for five years on this project [the film 'Wild Delta'] which started out of love for this place, which is the space in Romania with the greatest biodiversity. Because it started out of love for the delta, to us it was important that before the presence of the film in cinemas it was seen for free by those who call the Danube Delta home,' the film's producer, Matei Truta, told AGERPRES. The screening will be offered free of charge in the next few days at Mahmudia, Jurilovca and Sarichioi, coming to Romanian cinemas in the last ten days of October.
